articles.title: Why chatbots get things wrong

body.support:
Chatbots like ChatGPT can answer questions fast. They can explain things. They can give you ideas.

But a chatbot **guesses** which words come next. It doesn't check facts like a person does. So it can sound sure and still be **wrong**. Sometimes it even makes things up.

AI can make fake pictures too. A **deepfake** is a fake photo or video of a real person.

Four rules:

1. **Use it** for ideas and explaining.
2. **Check it.** Check facts on a website you can trust.
3. **Credit it.** Say when you used AI. Handing in AI work as your own is **plagiarism**.
4. **Protect it.** Don't type in your address or passwords. Never make fake pictures of real people.
body.core:
AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot and Meta AI can answer almost any question in seconds. They can explain a hard idea in simple words, give you ideas for a project, or write practice questions. That's useful.

But here's how they work. A chatbot has learned patterns from a huge amount of text. When you ask it something, it writes an answer by **predicting which words are likely to come next**. It doesn't check facts the way a person looks things up. So it can give you an answer that sounds **confident, friendly and completely wrong**. When AI makes up facts, quotes or references, it's called a **hallucination**.

AI image and video tools have a similar problem. They can make pictures of things that never happened, and fake photos, videos or voices of real people, called **deepfakes**.

Four rules keep you in control:

1. **Use it** for the right jobs: explaining, ideas, planning, practice. Not for facts you'll rely on, or for doing your work for you.
2. **Check it.** Any fact that matters (a time, a date, a rule, a number, a quote) needs checking against a **reliable source**, like an official website.
3. **Credit it.** Follow your school's rules, and say when and how you used AI. Handing in AI writing as your own is **plagiarism**.
4. **Protect it.** Don't type in your address, passwords, or photos and details of other people. And never make fake images of real people: it can hurt them badly, and some kinds are crimes.
body.extend:
Generative AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot and Meta AI can explain, summarise, brainstorm and draft in seconds. Used well, they're powerful learning tools.

Their weakness comes from how they work. A large language model is trained on vast amounts of text and generates a response by **predicting likely next words**. It doesn't verify claims the way a researcher would. The result is text that is fluent and confident in tone whether or not it's accurate. When a model invents facts, quotes or references, it's called a **hallucination**, and the confident tone makes it easy to miss.

Image, video and voice generators raise a related problem: realistic content of events that never happened, and **deepfakes** of real people.

Four rules keep you in control:

1. **Use it** for jobs that suit it: explaining, generating ideas, planning, practice. Not as a final source of facts, and not as a substitute for your own work.
2. **Check it.** Verify any fact that matters against a **reliable source**, ideally an official or primary one.
3. **Credit it.** Follow your school's or workplace's rules and acknowledge when and how you used AI. Submitting AI-generated work as your own is **plagiarism**.
4. **Protect it.** Keep personal information, passwords and other people's images out of AI tools. Creating fake images of real people can cause serious harm, and some kinds are criminal offences.

caseStudies.title: Even experts get caught

body.support:
In 2025, a big company called **Deloitte** wrote a report for the government. The government paid about **$440,000**.

A university teacher named **Chris Rudge** read it carefully. He found problems. Some of the research it talked about **did not exist**. It had a **made-up quote** too.

A new version of the report said **AI** had been used to help write it.

Deloitte agreed to **pay back some of the money**.

Nobody checked, until one careful reader did.
body.core:
In 2025, a federal government department paid a big consulting company, **Deloitte**, about **$440,000** to write a report on part of the welfare system.

After the report was published, **Chris Rudge**, an academic at the University of Sydney, read it closely. He found problems. Some of the **research papers it referred to didn't exist**. It also had a **made-up quote** from a court case.

A corrected version of the report was published. It now said that **generative AI** had been used to help write it. Deloitte said the changes didn't affect the report's findings.

Deloitte agreed to **pay back part of the money** it had been paid.

A big company, a government department, a lot of money, and nobody checked the references until one careful reader did.
body.extend:
In 2025, the federal **Department of Employment and Workplace Relations** paid the consultancy **Deloitte** about **$440,000** to review part of the welfare system.

After the report came out, University of Sydney academic **Chris Rudge** read it closely and found serious problems. It cited **academic works that did not exist**. It also included a **fabricated quote** from a court judgment.

A revised version was published later. It disclosed that a **generative AI** model had been used to help prepare the report. Deloitte said the corrections didn't change the findings, but it agreed to **refund part of the fee**.

The case is a warning about reliability. AI-generated references look exactly like real ones. The only defence is checking, and here the checking was done by an outside reader, after the report was already public.

source.name: The Register — “Deloitte refunds Aussie gov after AI fabrications slip into $440K welfare report” (October 2025)

teacher.overview: Students learn how AI chatbots generate text (predicting likely words), why that makes them confidently wrong at times, and four rules for using them: use it, check it, credit it, protect it. They annotate a made-up wrong chatbot answer, sort uses, check claims against reliable sources, study the 2025 Deloitte report case, write an AI-use note, and test a real chatbot before agreeing class AI rules in discussion.
prep: Check your school's and the Department's generative AI policy, and which AI tools (if any) students may use. Many public chatbots have age limits in their terms.
If students can't use a tool, prepare **screenshots** of a chatbot answering 6–8 checkable questions (include a couple of wrong answers: they're easy to get).
Have a device per pair for checking sources.
Find your school's founding year for the Check it table.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** it predicts which words are likely to come next; it doesn't check facts. Rules: use it, check it, credit it, protect it. Hallucination = AI making up facts, quotes or references; deepfake = a fake photo, video or voice of a real person. Never type: address, passwords, other people's photos or details.

**Wrong answer:** 1 the question (checkable); 2 confident but wrong (it's 16 in Victoria); 3 friendly tone (not proof); 4 reference that may not exist; 5 made-up extra; 6 no link or date.

**Sort:** gross pay — good use; last train — check it first; whole essay — don't (plagiarism); fake photo of teacher — don't; project ideas — good use; expert quotes — check it first (they may be made up).

**Check it:** 8 states — wrong (6 states and 2 mainland territories), check an official government site; Kosciuszko — right, check a reliable reference such as a national parks or government site; school year — check the school website or office.

**Case study:** references to research that didn't exist and a made-up court quote, found by Chris Rudge (University of Sydney); AI references look real and nobody checked; it should have said from the start that AI was used, and every reference should have been checked.

realityCheck: **Access varies.** Many schools restrict public chatbots, and many have age limits in their terms. Use a school-approved tool, or run the course on your own screenshots. It works almost as well.

**Wrong answers are easy to find, but not guaranteed.** Chatbots change often. Test your hook questions the day before; local questions (bus times, your school's history, local sport) are most likely to trip them up.

**Deepfakes can be a live issue.** If the discussion turns to fake nude images or image-based abuse, follow your school's procedures. eSafety can help get content removed, and making or sharing sexual deepfakes can be a criminal offence for under-18s.
**Don't make it anti-AI.** Students will use these tools at work. The goal is judgement: when to use it, when to check, and when to say so.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Catching a chatbot out is genuinely motivating, and the class rules make a useful display.
